name: The Law of Requisite Variety
statement: To control a system, a regulator must command at least as much variety as the disturbances it has to counter.
statementAccent: at least as much variety as the disturbances it has to counter
meaning: The law of requisite variety, formulated by the cybernetician W. Ross Ashby, states that to regulate or control a system a controller must be able to produce at least as much variety, the number of distinguishable states or responses, as the disturbances it must counteract. Ashby named it in the slogan only variety can destroy variety, later popularised by Stafford Beer as only variety can absorb variety. The point is that a regulator cannot push the variety of outcomes below a limit set by how the variety of disturbances compares with the variety of its own responses: to hold things steady against a varied world, the controller must itself be varied enough.
mechanism: Ashby measures variety as the count of distinguishable states, or its logarithm in bits, which turns the regulator into a communication channel and links the law to Shannon's information theory: the amount of regulation achievable cannot exceed the channel capacity the regulator commands. In logarithmic terms the residual variety in outcomes is at least the disturbance variety minus the regulator variety, so cutting the spread of outcomes requires raising the regulator's variety. Stafford Beer turned this into variety engineering for organisations, balancing the two sides either by attenuating the incoming variety of the environment or by amplifying the controller's own repertoire of responses until they match.

examples.text: A controller can only counter disturbances it can sense and respond to; a thermostat blind to a heat source it cannot detect or act on cannot regulate against it.

Beer's Viable System Model builds on the law: an organisation managing a complex market needs internally at least as much variety, in roles, options, and channels, as the environment throws at it, or it must attenuate that variety.

The related Conant-Ashby theorem of 1970 argues that every good regulator of a system must be a model of that system, extending the idea that effective control requires internal complexity matched to the task.

variants.name: Attenuate or amplify
variants.text: Beer's two levers of variety engineering: reduce the variety coming from the environment, or increase the controller's response variety, to bring the two into balance.

variants.name: The good regulator theorem
variants.text: Conant and Ashby's 1970 result that a maximally successful and simplest regulator must be isomorphic to the system it regulates, so it embodies a model of that system.

whyItMatters: Requisite variety is a foundational law of cybernetics and systems thinking, giving a precise sense to the intuition that you cannot control what you cannot match in complexity. It underpins management cybernetics and organisational design through Beer's work, informs the regulation of ecosystems, economies, and safety-critical systems, and frames a recurring lesson: when a controller is overwhelmed by a more varied environment, it must either grow its own repertoire or cut the variety it faces. It connects control, information theory, and organisation under a single, portable inequality.

working.text: ensure a controller's range of responses is at least as large as the range of disturbances it must handle, or control will fail.
when overwhelmed, either reduce the variety of what the environment sends you or expand your own repertoire, Beer's two levers.
recognise, with the good-regulator theorem, that effective control tends to require an internal model of the system being controlled.

limits: Requisite variety is a formal theorem within a specific model, of finite states, disturbances, and responses with the regulator treated as a channel, and within that model it is rigorously true. Applied to social, organisational, and political systems it becomes a looser analogy rather than a proof, since variety in a human organisation is rarely cleanly countable and the neat inequality turns into a heuristic. The interpretation of the related good-regulator theorem is itself contested, and its strong readings go beyond what the mathematics clearly establishes. Much of the popular management vocabulary of variety engineering is Beer's elaboration rather than Ashby's original statement.
misreadings: It does not say more complexity is always better; it sets a minimum matching requirement, and Beer's practical advice is often to reduce, or attenuate, incoming variety rather than only to add more. Ashby's own slogan is only variety can destroy variety; the common only variety can absorb variety is Beer's restatement of the same idea. It is a formal, mathematical result about counts of states and channel capacity, not an empirical law of nature. And requisite variety is distinct from the good-regulator theorem: they are related results from 1956 and 1970, not the same claim.
origin: Formulated by W. Ross Ashby in 'An Introduction to Cybernetics' (1956), where he named it 'only variety can destroy variety', and extended in management cybernetics by Stafford Beer and in the 1970 Conant-Ashby good-regulator theorem.
